title: Recasting DiT for Extreme Image Compression with Hierarchical Visual Priors

paper.title: Recasting DiT for Extreme Image Compression with Hierarchical Visual Priors
paper.abstract: Abstract Pretrained diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for extreme image compression, but their stochastic, iterative generation processes are not designed to decode compressed representations directly. We present PrismCodec, which recasts a pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) as a bitstream-grounded one-step generative decoder. PrismCodec uses the decoded representation in two complementary roles: a projected codec state defines the starting state for generation, while hierarchical visual priors derived from the same decoded latent provide semantic and structural guidance. To bridge the gap between stochastic, iterative generation and deterministic one-step decoding, we develop a progressive adaptation strategy. We first learn codec-conditioned transport from a noisy neighborhood centered on the codec state, distill it into a one-step mapping, and finally anneal the source perturbation to zero during end-to-end optimization. The resulting decoder reconstructs deterministically from the received representation without additional conditioning bits. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec consistently improves rate–perception performance over prior generative codecs, achieving BD-rate reductions of 70 70 – 75 % 75\% in LPIPS and 75 75 – 81 % 81\% in DISTS over StableCodec. Code will be released upon acceptance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: At ultra-low bitrates, learned codecs built on optimized transforms and entropy models [ 4 , 5 , 76 ] can preserve only limited visual evidence of the source image. Generative compression therefore relies on image generation priors to synthesize details that are not explicitly transmitted. Yet compression differs fundamentally from unconstrained generation: plausible content is insufficient if it is inconsistent with the evidence retained in the bitstream. A central challenge is therefore to exploit powerful generative priors while grounding reconstruction in this limited transmitted evidence. Pretrained diffusion and flow models offer powerful visual priors [ 37 , 88 , 83 , 28 ] , but their generative processes are not naturally aligned with compression decoding. Existing methods expose image-specific compressed evidence to the generative decoder through different interfaces. OneDC [ 112 ] and DiT-IC [ 93 ] derive semantic guidance directly from compressed representations, while AEIC [ 123 ] removes the text-conditioning pathway and reconstructs from codec latents. NeFIC [ 17 ] and StableCodec [ 122 ] retain fixed text conditions but also inject image-specific information through a decoded anchor and a codec latent, respectively. Together, these approaches show that effective generative decoding depends on how transmitted visual evidence is exposed to the generator. Two questions nevertheless remain: how should that evidence determine both the generative starting state and the visual guidance, and how can a pretrained model built for stochastic, iterative generation be adapted to deterministic one-step decoding? We introduce PrismCodec , which recasts a pretrained DiT as a compression decoder whose starting state and visual guidance are both derived from the bitstream. These two roles are complementary: the codec-centered state anchors generation in the transmitted representation, while the visual priors specify semantic content and spatial structure that should be preserved during reconstruction. Inspired by recent image-generation studies [ 94 , 31 ] , we combine semantic and structural visual priors through a shared visual-evidence pathway. A lightweight decoder renders the decoded codec features as an internal evidence image, providing a common image-domain interface through which pretrained visual encoders can interpret the same bitstream-derived evidence. DINOv3 [ 95 ] supplies multi-depth dense semantic features, which are delivered to successive DiT block groups through depth-matched cross-attention rather than collapsed into a single condition. This preserves complementary levels of visual abstraction across the pretrained representation hierarchy. In parallel, the diffusion-native VAE supplies a spatially aligned structural prior through the latent-input pathway. Both priors are computed entirely at the decoder and therefore require no additional conditioning bits. Visual conditioning alone, however, does not make a pretrained generator a practical compression decoder. Diffusion and flow models are typically trained to generate from stochastic sources through iterative transport, whereas practical compression typically favors deterministic reconstruction from a transmitted representation under a tight decoding budget. We therefore progressively reshape the generative process around the codec state. First, we learn conditional transport from a stochastic neighborhood centered on the codec representation to the clean generative latent, so that the learned trajectory is already grounded in transmitted evidence rather than generic noise. We then distill this codec-conditioned transport into a direct one-step mapping. Finally, during end-to-end compression training, we gradually contract the stochastic source distribution onto the deterministic codec state. This annealing avoids an abrupt shift from the stochastic source used for flow learning and distillation to the deterministic input used at deployment, while allowing the codec and generative decoder to adapt jointly. Fig. 1 summarizes the resulting rate–perception performance. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec achieves LPIPS and DISTS BD-rate reductions of approximately 70 70 – 75 % 75\% and 75 75 – 81 % 81\% , respectively, over StableCodec. Our main contributions are: • We recast a pretrained DiT as a bitstream-grounded generative decoder, using the compressed representation to determine both its starting state and its visual guidance. • We introduce hierarchical visual priors that combine multi-depth dense semantic features with a diffusion-native structural prior through complementary DiT conditioning interfaces. • We develop a progressive adaptation strategy that moves from codec-centered stochastic flow learning through one-step distillation to deterministic end-to-end decoding, bridging pretrained stochastic generation and practical extreme image compression.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Generative Image Compression. Generative codecs use learned priors to recover plausible content at very low bitrates. Adversarial methods improve perceptual quality through distribution matching [ 74 , 78 ] , while conditional and residual diffusion reconstruct images from compressed representations [ 113 , 30 ] . Recent work increasingly adapts pretrained generative priors, making bitstream grounding and efficient decoding central design concerns. The decoded feature 𝐟 c \mathbf{f}_{c} yields a codec state 𝐳 c \mathbf{z}_{c} and an evidence image 𝐱 ~ \widetilde{\mathbf{x}} for two frozen encoders. DINOv3 supplies multi-depth dense semantic priors 𝐏 sem \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}} to successive DiT groups through depth-matched cross-attention. The VAE encoder supplies a spatially aligned structural prior 𝐏 str \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}} , channel-concatenated with 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} . The codec-centered sampler interpolates between the clean latent and a noisy source centered on 𝐳 c \mathbf{z}_{c} . Bitstream Grounding and One-Step Adaptation. Pretrained-prior codecs expose transmitted evidence through different conditioning interfaces to guide reconstruction [ 122 , 17 , 18 ] . StableCodec combines a codec latent with structural correction under fixed text conditioning. OneDC [ 112 ] derives tokenizer-supervised semantic tokens from the hyperprior, DiT-IC [ 93 ] uses text-aligned compressed features, and AEIC [ 123 ] removes cross-attention. PrismCodec instead separates bitstream-derived evidence into two roles: a codec state determines the generative source, while an evidence image provides hierarchical semantic and diffusion-native structural guidance through complementary pretrained encoders and separate DiT conditioning interfaces. Fast decoding is addressed through diffusion pretraining and distillation. CoD [ 44 ] pretrains diffusion for compression, CoD-Lite [ 43 ] introduces lightweight one-step decoding, OSCAR [ 33 ] supports one-step reconstruction across multiple bitrates, and FlowCodec [ 40 ] adapts a pretrained flow prior for near-terminal transport. More detailed comparisons with prior methods are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.1 Overview
sections.text: PrismCodec recasts a pretrained DiT as a one-step generative decoder whose reconstruction is grounded in the received bitstream. Given a source image 𝐱 \mathbf{x} encoded into a bitstream 𝐛 \mathbf{b} , entropy decoding produces compressed features from which we derive two complementary forms of information: a codec state 𝐳 c \mathbf{z}_{c} that determines the starting state for generation, and visual priors 𝒫 \mathcal{P} that specify the semantic content and spatial structure to preserve during reconstruction. The decoder computes 𝐳 ^ 0 = 𝒢 θ ​ ( 𝐳 c , 𝒫 ) , 𝐱 ^ = 𝒟 g ​ ( 𝐳 ^ 0 ) , \widehat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}=\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{c};\mathcal{P}),\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{D}_{g}(\widehat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}), (1) where 𝒢 θ \mathcal{G}_{\theta} is a one-step latent mapping implemented by a DiT, and 𝒟 g \mathcal{D}_{g} maps the predicted latent back to image space through the generative VAE decoder, kept frozen throughout all stages. A pretrained diffusion model, however, is designed for stochastic, iterative generation rather than deterministic decoding from a transmitted representation. We therefore adapt the generative process progressively. Stage I learns conditional transport from a stochastic neighborhood centered on the codec state, grounding the generative trajectory in transmitted evidence. Stage II distills this codec-conditioned transport into a one-step map. Stage III then contracts the remaining source randomness while jointly optimizing the codec and generator, continuously aligning the training-time source with the deterministic codec state used at deployment. Fig. 2 illustrates the visual interface and Stage-I adaptation, while Fig. 3 summarizes Stages II and III. Appendix B summarizes the notation.

sections.heading: 3.3 Hierarchical Visual Priors
sections.text: The evidence image is interpreted through two complementary pretrained representation spaces. Multi-depth DINOv3 features provide dense semantic guidance, while the diffusion-native VAE provides a reference in the generator’s native latent space [ 94 , 31 ] . Both priors are derived from 𝐱 ~ \widetilde{\mathbf{x}} at the decoder and therefore introduce no additional conditioning bits. Multi-depth dense semantic prior. We extract spatial patch tokens from L L selected depths of a frozen DINOv3 transformer, excluding class and register tokens. After per-depth normalization and learned projection, they form 𝐏 sem = ℋ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ~ ) = ( 𝐏 1 sem , … , 𝐏 L sem ) , \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}}=\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}})=\bigl(\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{L}\bigr), (4) where each 𝐏 ℓ sem \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}}_{\ell} is a dense spatial token sequence projected to the DiT hidden dimension. Rather than collapsing the selected DINOv3 depths into a single condition, we preserve their ordering and assign successive semantic levels to successive groups of DiT blocks through cross-attention. This depth-matched design exposes the generator to complementary levels of visual abstraction throughout the network. Diffusion-native structural prior. The semantic branch does not directly provide a reference in the native latent coordinates used by the generator. We therefore encode the same evidence image with the frozen native VAE encoder. Let 𝒮 \mathcal{S} denote the encoder with its fixed latent calibration. We define 𝐏 str = 𝒮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ~ ) , 𝐳 0 = 𝒮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}}=\mathcal{S}(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}),\qquad\mathbf{z}_{0}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{x}), (5) where 𝐏 str \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}} is the structural prior and 𝐳 0 \mathbf{z}_{0} is the clean latent used as the training target. Because 𝐏 str \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}} lies in the same latent coordinates as the generative state, it provides spatially aligned guidance complementary to the semantic tokens. Its role is distinct from that of 𝐳 c \mathbf{z}_{c} : the codec state defines the source from which transport begins, whereas 𝐏 str \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}} acts as a structural reference throughout the generative mapping. Complementary conditioning. The complete visual condition is 𝒫 = ( 𝐏 str , 𝐏 sem ) \mathcal{P}=(\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}},\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sem}}) . The two priors enter the DiT through distinct interfaces: 𝐏 str \mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{str}} is concatenated with the evolving latent before patch embedding, whereas the assigned semantic tokens are injected through cross-attention. We denote the resulting predictor by 𝐮 θ ​ ( 𝐳 , t , r , 𝒫 ) \mathbf{u}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},t,r;\mathcal{P}) , where t t and r r denote the current and destination flow times, respectively. Both conditioning paths remain active throughout adaptation and deployment.

sections.heading: 3.4 Learning a One-Step Generative Decoder
sections.text: The pretrained generator and the deployed codec differ along two coupled axes: the former starts from a stochastic source and follows iterative transport, whereas the latter must start from a bitstream-determined state and decode in one deterministic step. Rather than imposing both changes at once, we adapt the generative process progressively. Stage I re-centers the source on the codec state while retaining stochasticity for flow learning; Stage II distills the resulting codec-conditioned transport into a one-step map; and Stage III contracts the remaining source randomness while jointly adapting the complete compression system to its deployed deterministic input.

sections.text: Following Yao et al. [114] , we pretrain a class-conditional LightningDiT on ImageNet-1K [ 20 ] for 100 epochs, and then add visual cross-attention layers for Stage I adaptation. Following DiT-IC [ 93 ] , we train on high-quality images from CLIC 2020 Professional [ 99 ] , MLIC-Train-100K [ 46 ] , and LSDIR [ 60 ] , retaining images whose height and width both exceed 512 pixels. We use aspect-ratio buckets centered on a nominal 768 × 768 768\times 768 resolution, spanning ratios from 1 : 2 1{:}2 to 2 : 1 2{:}1 . Before Stage I, we pretrain the codec and evidence path for 20k updates using the evidence MSE and DINO losses to obtain a stable initialization, with the same weights as Stage I: λ ev I = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{ev}}^{\mathrm{I}}=1 and λ ev ​ - ​ sem = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{ev\mbox{-}sem}}=0.5 . sections.heading: 4.1.2 Datasets, Metrics, and Baselines
sections.text: We evaluate on Kodak [ 24 ] (24 images), the CLIC2020 test set [ 99 ] (428 images), and the DIV2K validation set [ 1 ] (100 images). We report PSNR and MS-SSIM [ 104 ] for distortion, LPIPS [ 121 ] and DISTS [ 21 ] for perceptual fidelity, and FID [ 36 ] for distributional realism. The four paired metrics are computed on full-resolution RGB reconstructions and averaged over images; FID uses 256 × 256 256\times 256 patches on CLIC2020 and DIV2K, following Mentzer et al. [74] . We omit FID on Kodak given its small sample size. We compare with DiffC [ 102 ] , ResULIC [ 49 ] , DLF [ 111 ] , OSCAR [ 33 ] , StableCodec [ 122 ] , OneDC [ 112 ] , AEIC-ME [ 123 ] , DiT-IC [ 93 ] , and CoD-Lite [ 43 ] . We summarize bitrate efficiency with BD-rate [ 7 ] , using StableCodec as the reference. Negative BD-rate indicates bitrate savings at equal quality.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Quantitative Evaluation
sections.text: The main comparison tests whether grounding both the generative source and visual guidance in the received bitstream translates into a better rate–perception tradeoff without systematically sacrificing source fidelity. Fig. 4 reports the rate–distortion and rate–perception curves in the ultra-low-bitrate regime, while Table 1 summarizes BD-rates relative to StableCodec.

sections.heading: Perceptual fidelity and realism.
sections.text: Across all three datasets, PrismCodec shifts the LPIPS and DISTS curves favorably relative to prior generative codecs. On CLIC2020, it reduces bitrate relative to StableCodec by 71.46% at matched LPIPS and 77.08% at matched DISTS; the corresponding savings on DIV2K are 69.54% and 74.64%. The same operating points also yield FID-based savings of 30.63% and 46.96% on CLIC2020 and DIV2K, respectively, indicating that the gains in paired perceptual fidelity are accompanied by improved distributional realism. Appendix D provides complementary KID comparisons.

sections.heading: Source fidelity.
sections.text: The perceptual gains do not come with a systematic loss in distortion performance. PrismCodec achieves PSNR-based bitrate savings of 5.82%, 30.45%, and 17.21% on Kodak, CLIC2020, and DIV2K, respectively. MS-SSIM remains close to StableCodec, with a 0.40% bitrate increase on Kodak and reductions of 1.48% and 0.90% on CLIC2020 and DIV2K. Taken together, these results support the central premise of PrismCodec: bitstream-grounded generation can improve perceptual reconstruction while retaining source-dependent fidelity. sections.heading: 4.2.2 Qualitative Evaluation
sections.text: Fig. 5 examines whether the quantitative gains correspond to source-specific visual details rather than only aggregate metric improvements. At lower bitrates than the compared baselines, PrismCodec better preserves plate lettering (DIV2K 0847), leaf-tip contours and serrations (DIV2K 0857), and the fox’s eye, nose, and fur patterns (DIV2K 0862), whereas several baselines smooth or alter these details. These examples are qualitatively consistent with the intended role of visual evidence in constraining generative reconstruction. Appendix F provides additional comparisons.

sections.heading: 4.3 Efficiency Evaluation
sections.text: We report deployed parameters, encoding and decoding latency, and computation (kMACs/pixel and FLOPs) in Table 2 . Measurements use synthetic RGB inputs at 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 , batch size one, and an NVIDIA A100 GPU; after warm-up, latency is averaged over 30 CUDA-synchronized runs. PrismCodec decodes a 2K image in 2.10 s, compared with 9.74 s for StableCodec and 3.22 s for OSCAR, while remaining in the same order of total computation as these two generative baselines.

sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation Studies
sections.text: We organize the ablations around the three claims underlying PrismCodec: (i) semantic and structural visual priors provide complementary guidance, with multi-depth semantics contributing beyond a single representation level; (ii) transmitted evidence should determine the generative source as well as its conditions; and (iii) explicit one-step distillation and subsequent source contraction are both important for adapting stochastic generation to deterministic decoding. All results report LPIPS- and DISTS-based BD-rate (%) on DIV2K relative to StableCodec. Each variant trains its own high-rate model and uses matched fine-tuning schedules to obtain the five rate points in Sec. 4.1 .

sections.heading: Hierarchical visual priors.
sections.text: Table 4 separates two aspects of the proposed conditioning design. First, Single semantic depth repeats the final selected DINOv3 layer across all four DiT groups, increasing LPIPS- and DISTS-based BD-rate by 9.90 and 6.27 percentage points relative to the full model. This isolates the benefit of preserving multiple representation depths rather than collapsing semantic guidance to one level. Second, Structural only removes semantic guidance and increases the two BD-rates by 17.87 and 16.32 points, while Semantic only removes structural input conditioning and increases them by 26.65 and 27.40 points. The degradation in both single-branch variants supports the complementary roles of dense semantic guidance and diffusion-native structural guidance.

sections.heading: Bitstream-grounded source.
sections.text: With both priors retained, Zero-centered noise replaces the codec-centered source with a Gaussian-noise starting state and performs worse than both the stochastic codec-centered variant ( w/o annealing ) and the full model (Table 4 ). Thus, the gain from 𝐳 c \mathbf{z}_{c} is not merely duplicated by the conditioning paths: exposing the bitstream through the generative source provides an additional and complementary form of grounding.

sections.heading: Progressive adaptation to deterministic decoding.
sections.text: Table 4 evaluates the two transitions from the Stage-I iterative flow to deterministic one-step decoding. w/o annealing keeps ρ = 1 \rho=1 through Stage III and inference, using 𝐳 c + 0.3 ​ ϵ \mathbf{z}_{c}+0.3\boldsymbol{\epsilon} as the source, and increases LPIPS- and DISTS-based BD-rates by 14.52 and 20.23 points. This shows that the stochastic distilled source should be contracted to the deterministic codec state before deployment. w/o distillation skips Stage II and directly fine-tunes the Stage-I model with the full model’s annealing schedule, increasing the two BD-rates by 14.80 and 16.60 points. Together, these results support both flow-map distillation and source-noise annealing in the transition to deterministic one-step decoding.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented PrismCodec, which recasts a pretrained DiT as a bitstream-grounded one-step decoder for extreme image compression. The compressed representation determines both the generative starting state and hierarchical semantic and structural guidance. Through codec-centered flow adaptation, flow-map distillation, and source-noise annealing, PrismCodecprogressively transforms stochastic iterative generation into deterministic one-step decoding. The resulting model reconstructs directly from the received bitstream without additional conditioning bits, yielding an efficient and effective rate–perception tradeoff.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: This appendix expands the positioning in Sec. 2 . We first place PrismCodec within learned and generative image compression, and then compare the closest pretrained-prior codecs along the same two questions that motivate our method: how bitstream-derived evidence enters the generator and how stochastic generation is adapted to one-step reconstruction .

sections.heading: A.1 Conventional Learned Compression
sections.text: Learned codecs have advanced through stronger entropy models [ 75 , 34 , 35 , 85 , 47 , 46 , 19 , 22 ] , more expressive transforms [ 57 , 68 , 119 , 106 , 13 , 16 , 15 , 59 ] , and specialized, scalable, or distilled designs for efficiency [ 127 , 103 , 105 , 70 , 61 , 62 , 14 , 58 , 124 , 65 ] . These approaches improve the coded representation itself; PrismCodec instead focuses on how a pretrained generative prior should decode the limited evidence that remains after extreme compression.

sections.heading: A.2 Broader Generative Compression
sections.text: Generative codecs introduce learned priors to recover visually plausible content at low rates. Existing families use adversarial priors [ 32 , 3 , 74 , 78 , 2 , 50 , 41 ] , discrete representations [ 101 , 27 , 25 , 73 , 110 , 42 ] , or complementary representations [ 71 , 111 , 126 , 66 ] ; related work also studies bitrate control, progressive decoding, and rate–distortion-optimized quantization [ 56 , 125 , 9 , 45 ] . Diffusion-based codecs reconstruct from compressed information through conditional denoising [ 98 , 113 , 38 ] , residual generation [ 30 , 64 ] , or pretrained generative priors [ 84 , 8 , 86 , 48 ] . Other methods learn latent guidance and reconstruction corrections [ 63 , 72 , 107 , 109 , 49 , 11 ] , or use frozen priors for zero-shot coding [ 102 , 108 , 26 , 80 , 100 ] ; recent work further connects diffusion noise with quantization [ 87 , 23 ] . CoD pretrains diffusion specifically for compression [ 44 ] , and CoD-Lite combines this with a lightweight one-step convolutional decoder [ 43 ] . Accelerated sampling and distillation [ 96 , 90 , 91 , 116 , 115 ] also motivate one-step codecs [ 33 , 82 ] , while FlowCodec uses LoRA-adapted flow priors for near-terminal one-step latent transport with an empty prompt [ 40 , 39 ] . A second line of work concerns the conditioning interface. Text-guided codecs transmit descriptions or learn language-aligned representations [ 55 , 10 , 51 , 52 , 54 , 81 , 97 ] , and CADC derives text from reconstructions [ 92 ] . Image conditions are also widely used for controlled generation and restoration [ 120 , 77 , 118 , 12 ] , while REPA aligns diffusion hidden states with pretrained visual features during training [ 117 ] . For the closest compression methods, Table 5 summarizes how the transmitted representation determines the generator input and conditions, together with the mechanism used for one-step adaptation. The categories below concern the explicit conditioning pathway; all methods also receive image-specific information from their coded representations. sections.heading: A.3 Fixed Text Conditions
sections.text: StableCodec [ 122 ] adapts SD-Turbo with a fixed prompt and a codec-produced latent input. Its auxiliary encoder supplies source features during compression, and an auxiliary decoder predicts a structural residual that is added after denoising and before VAE decoding. The fixed prompt therefore coexists with substantial image-specific guidance. PrismCodec separates the same broad grounding problem into distinct roles: a codec-centered source determines where generation starts, while a frozen VAE latent and multi-depth visual tokens provide structural and semantic guidance through separate DiT interfaces. StableCodec also tightens the rate penalty during training; PrismCodec’s source contraction instead changes the generator’s input distribution as it approaches deterministic deployment. NeFIC [ 17 ] also retains a fixed prompt, using a decoded anchor for conditioning and a codec-derived bypass latent as the input to its video-diffusion generator.

sections.heading: A.4 Learned Semantic Surrogates: OneDC and DiT-IC
sections.text: OneDC [ 112 ] decodes a semantic token sequence from the quantized hyperprior and uses it as cross-attention context. A pretrained generative tokenizer supplies training labels through an auxiliary prediction task; the tokenizer and predictor are unnecessary at inference. The resulting hyperprior tokens retain spatial locality. PrismCodec instead computes semantic conditions from an evidence image at decoding time, preserves patch-token sets from multiple pretrained depths, and assigns them to successive DiT block groups. This makes the semantic hierarchy an explicit inference-time condition. OneDC additionally uses diffusion distillation for perceptual refinement; its tokenizer supervision and refinement therefore address different roles from PrismCodec’s Stage-II flow-map distillation. DiT-IC [ 93 ] projects compressed features into the text conditioning space and uses contrastive alignment with text embeddings during training; inference uses the latent condition alone. Its adaptation also includes a variance-derived spatial pseudo-timestep and self-distillation that aligns reconstructed latents with frozen encoder outputs. PrismCodec preserves multiple visual representation depths and adds a separate diffusion-native VAE structural condition. Its one-step adaptation also follows a different path: Stage I first learns continuous conditional transport around the codec state, and Stage II distills the resulting finite-time map. The source perturbation scale therefore defines a Gaussian neighborhood of the transmitted codec state, whereas DiT-IC’s pseudo-timestep controls spatially varying reconstruction strength.

sections.heading: A.5 Removing the Cross-Attention Pathway: AEIC
sections.text: AEIC [ 123 ] simplifies the SD-Turbo denoiser by removing the text encoder, timestep embeddings, and cross-attention layers. Its codec synthesis transform produces both a denoising input and a structural residual, so reconstruction still depends on image-specific compressed information. Dual-side feature distillation transfers knowledge from a moderate-encoder model to shallow-encoder variants. This targets encoder efficiency and feature preservation. PrismCodec retains explicit visual cross-attention and adapts a time-dependent conditional flow before distilling its map in Stage II. The two uses of distillation therefore solve different problems: AEIC targets encoder efficiency and feature transfer, whereas PrismCodec compresses an already bitstream-grounded generative transport into one step.

sections.heading: A.6 Auxiliary Reconstruction Guidance: SODEC
sections.text: SODEC [ 18 ] is closely related to our use of a decoded image as a visual interface. Its fidelity decoder reconstructs an auxiliary image from compressed latents; a frozen ViT and a learned projection produce a cross-attention condition. A separate transform supplies the input to an SD2.1 U-Net evaluated at a fixed timestep. Both methods therefore derive visual guidance and the generative input from the bitstream. PrismCodec further separates the conditioning role into two pretrained representation spaces: semantic features remain distinct across DINOv3 depths, while a diffusion-native VAE latent provides spatially aligned structural guidance. The shared evidence image gives both encoders a common image-domain view of the decoded evidence, and its auxiliary objective includes paired semantic supervision ( Appendix C.2 ). The adaptation mechanisms also differ. SODEC pretrains a high-bitrate codec, warms up the diffusion path, and then tightens the rate penalty during joint optimization. PrismCodec instead learns codec-centered conditional transport, distills that transport into a one-step map, and then contracts the stochastic source onto the deterministic codec state. SODEC’s rate annealing changes the coding constraint; PrismCodec’s source-noise annealing changes the generator’s input distribution.

sections.heading: A.7 Visual Priors and Progressive Flow Adaptation
sections.text: PrismCodec’s semantic branch uses dense DINOv3 features [ 95 ] , while its structural branch uses the frozen VAE encoder. Both are explicit inference-time conditions derived from the same bitstream-dependent evidence image. This differs from representation-alignment methods such as REPA [ 117 ] , which use pretrained visual features as training supervision for diffusion hidden states. More generally, using semantic features in an auxiliary loss or discriminator is not equivalent to supplying those features as decoder-side visual context. The adaptation axis is likewise compositional. Stage I builds on flow matching and rectified flow [ 67 , 69 ] ; Stage II uses established AYF-EMD distillation with an interval-average velocity parameterization [ 89 , 29 ] . PMRF [ 79 ] provides a related precedent for centering a stochastic flow source on an informative deterministic estimate. PrismCodec instead centers the source on an entropy-decoded codec state, without a posterior-mean assumption or inherited PMRF optimality guarantee, and couples that source with hierarchical visual conditions. Stage III then specializes the distilled map to the deterministic codec state used at deployment (Sections 3.4.1 – 3.4.3 ).

sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: PrismCodecprioritizes rate–perception performance and effective adaptation of a pretrained generative prior, rather than minimizing model size. As a result, the current decoder remains relatively large compared with lightweight compression models. Moreover, high-resolution images are decoded with overlapping latent tiles to keep memory consumption manageable. These computational costs accompany the substantial rate–perception gains obtained by the current design, but leave clear opportunities for improving deployment efficiency. Future work will explore more compact generative decoders and architectures capable of processing full-resolution images directly without tiled inference, while preserving the benefits of bitstream-grounded one-step decoding.

We present PrismCodec, which recasts a pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) as a bitstream-grounded one-step generative decoder. PrismCodec uses the decoded representation in two complementary roles: a projected codec state defines the starting state for generation, while hierarchical visual priors derived from the same decoded latent provide semantic and structural guidance. To bridge the gap between stochastic, iterative generation and deterministic one-step decoding, we develop a progressive adaptation strategy. We first learn codec-conditioned transport from a noisy neighborhood centered on the codec state, distill it into a one-step mapping, and finally anneal the source perturbation to zero during end-to-end optimization. The resulting decoder reconstructs deterministically from the received representation without additional conditioning bits. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec consistently improves rate–perception performance over prior generative codecs, achieving BD-rate reductions of 70 70 – 75 % 75\% in LPIPS and 75 75 – 81 % 81\% in DISTS over StableCodec. Negative values indicate bitrate savings and extend to the right. Red arrows report PrismCodec’s direct BD-rate relative to StableCodec. Triangles mark bars clipped at the axis limit; labels retain the unclipped values, rounded to integers. 1 Introduction At ultra-low bitrates, learned codecs built on optimized transforms and entropy models [ 4 , 5 , 76 ] can preserve only limited visual evidence of the source image. Generative compression therefore relies on image generation priors to synthesize details that are not explicitly transmitted. Yet compression differs fundamentally from unconstrained generation: plausible content is insufficient if it is inconsistent with the evidence retained in the bitstream. A central challenge is therefore to exploit powerful generative priors while grounding reconstruction in this limited transmitted evidence. Pretrained diffusion and flow models offer powerful visual priors [ 37 , 88 , 83 , 28 ] , but their generative processes are not naturally aligned with compression decoding. Existing methods expose image-specific compressed evidence to the generative decoder through different interfaces. OneDC [ 112 ] and DiT-IC [ 93 ] derive semantic guidance directly from compressed representations, while AEIC [ 123 ] removes the text-conditioning pathway and reconstructs from codec latents. NeFIC [ 17 ] and StableCodec [ 122 ] retain fixed text conditions but also inject image-specific information through a decoded anchor and a codec latent, respectively. Together, these approaches show that effective generative decoding depends on how transmitted visual evidence is exposed to the generator. Two questions nevertheless remain: how should that evidence determine both the generative starting state and the visual guidance, and how can a pretrained model built for stochastic, iterative generation be adapted to deterministic one-step decoding? We introduce PrismCodec , which recasts a pretrained DiT as a compression decoder whose starting state and visual guidance are both derived from the bitstream. These two roles are complementary: the codec-centered state anchors generation in the transmitted representation, while the visual priors specify semantic content and spatial structure that should be preserved during reconstruction. Inspired by recent image-generation studies [ 94 , 31 ] , we combine semantic and structural visual priors through a shared visual-evidence pathway. A lightweight decoder renders the decoded codec features as an internal evidence image, providing a common image-domain interface through which pretrained visual encoders can interpret the same bitstream-derived evidence. DINOv3 [ 95 ] supplies multi-depth dense semantic features, which are delivered to successive DiT block groups through depth-matched cross-attention rather than collapsed into a single condition. This preserves complementary levels of visual abstraction across the pretrained representation hierarchy. In parallel, the diffusion-native VAE supplies a spatially aligned structural prior through the latent-input pathway. Both priors are computed entirely at the decoder and therefore require no additional conditioning bits. Visual conditioning alone, however, does not make a pretrained generator a practical compression decoder. Diffusion and flow models are typically trained to generate from stochastic sources through iterative transport, whereas practical compression typically favors deterministic reconstruction from a transmitted representation under a tight decoding budget. We therefore progressively reshape the generative process around the codec state. First, we learn conditional transport from a stochastic neighborhood centered on the codec representation to the clean generative latent, so that the learned trajectory is already grounded in transmitted evidence rather than generic noise. We then distill this codec-conditioned transport into a direct one-step mapping. Finally, during end-to-end compression training, we gradually contract the stochastic source distribution onto the deterministic codec state. This annealing avoids an abrupt shift from the stochastic source used for flow learning and distillation to the deterministic input used at deployment, while allowing the codec and generative decoder to adapt jointly. Fig. 1 summarizes the resulting rate–perception performance. Across Kodak, CLIC, and DIV2K, PrismCodec achieves LPIPS and DISTS BD-rate reductions of approximately 70 70 – 75 % 75\% and 75 75 – 81 % 81\% , respectively, over StableCodec. Our main contributions are: • We recast a pretrained DiT as a bitstream-grounded generative decoder, using the compressed representation to determine both its starting state and its visual guidance. • We introduce hierarchical visual priors that combine multi-depth dense semantic features with a diffusion-native structural prior through complementary DiT conditioning interfaces. • We develop a progressive adaptation strategy that moves from codec-centered stochastic flow learning through one-step distillation to deterministic end-to-end decoding, bridging pretrained stochastic generation and practical extreme image compression. 2 Related Work Generative Image Compression. Generative codecs use learned priors to recover plausible content at very low bitrates. Adversarial methods improve perceptual quality through distribution matching [ 74 , 78 ] , while conditional and residual diffusion reconstruct images from compressed representations [ 113 , 30 ] . Recent work increasingly adapts pretrained generative priors, making bitstream grounding and efficient decoding central design concerns. Pretrained-prior codecs expose transmitted evidence through different conditioning interfaces to guide reconstruction [ 122 , 17 , 18 ] . StableCodec combines a codec latent with structural correction under fixed text conditioning. OneDC [ 112 ] derives tokenizer-supervised semantic tokens from the hyperprior, DiT-IC [ 93 ] uses text-aligned compressed features, and AEIC [ 123 ] removes cross-attention. PrismCodec instead separates bitstream-derived evidence into two roles: a codec state determines the generative source, while an evidence image provides hierarchical semantic and diffusion-native structural guidance through complementary pretrained encoders and separate DiT conditioning interfaces. Fast decoding is addressed through diffusion pretraining and distillation. CoD [ 44 ] pretrains diffusion for compression, CoD-Lite [ 43 ] introduces lightweight one-step decoding, OSCAR [ 33 ] supports one-step reconstruction across multiple bitrates, and FlowCodec [ 40 ] adapts a pretrained flow prior for near-terminal transport. Fig. 4 reports the rate–distortion and rate–perception curves in the ultra-low-bitrate regime, while Table 1 summarizes BD-rates relative to StableCodec. Perceptual fidelity and realism. Across all three datasets, PrismCodec shifts the LPIPS and DISTS curves favorably relative to prior generative codecs. On CLIC2020, it reduces bitrate relative to StableCodec by 71.46% at matched LPIPS and 77.08% at matched DISTS; the corresponding savings on DIV2K are 69.54% and 74.64%. The same operating points also yield FID-based savings of 30.63% and 46.96% on CLIC2020 and DIV2K, respectively, indicating that the gains in paired perceptual fidelity are accompanied by improved distributional realism. Appendix D provides complementary KID comparisons. Source fidelity. The perceptual gains do not come with a systematic loss in distortion performance. PrismCodec achieves PSNR-based bitrate savings of 5.82%, 30.45%, and 17.21% on Kodak, CLIC2020, and DIV2K, respectively. MS-SSIM remains close to StableCodec, with a 0.40% bitrate increase on Kodak and reductions of 1.48% and 0.90% on CLIC2020 and DIV2K. Taken together, these results support the central premise of PrismCodec: bitstream-grounded generation can improve perceptual reconstruction while retaining source-dependent fidelity. The compressed representation determines both the generative starting state and hierarchical semantic and structural guidance. Through codec-centered flow adaptation, flow-map distillation, and source-noise annealing, PrismCodecprogressively transforms stochastic iterative generation into deterministic one-step decoding. The resulting model reconstructs directly from the received bitstream without additional conditioning bits, yielding an efficient and effective rate–perception tradeoff.
